newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator urges NATO to override Bosnia TV.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator urges NATO to override Bosnia TV.

text.p: An advanced U.S. aircraft that jams radio and television broadcasts should be sent to override ultra-nationalist Bosnian Serb programmes that depict NATO forces as the enemy, a top Senate Armed Services panel member said on Wednesday.

The craft, the EC-130E "Commando Solo," should broadcast alternative programming aimed at carrying out the Bosnia peace accords reached in Ohio more than a year and a half ago, Sen. Carl Levin of Michigan, the committee's top Democrat, said.
Levin said the EC-130 could counteract what he described as threatening broadcasts of a Bosnian Serb leadership still loyal to former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
"This distorted picture has been used to interfere with the implementation of the civilian aspects of the Dayton peace accords," he said in remarks prepared for delivery on the Senate floor.

The accords negotiated in the fall of 1995 in Dayton, Ohio, were designed to end 3-1/2 years of civil war. Continuing violations have led to fears that the United States and its NATO partners will not be able to withdraw their 31,000 troops -- or even most of them -- as currently scheduled, next June.

Levin said Karadzic and the state-controlled Bosnian Serb media had been orchestrating attacks on NATO forces since the seizure by British SAS troops of one Bosnian Serb war crimes suspect and the killing of another on July 10.
"The influence of Karadzic must be checked. I believe that his control of the Bosnian Serb media is a good place to start," the senator said.

"The beauty of Commando Solo is that its radio and television broadcasts will go into the homes of the Bosnian Serbs where they can receive it away from prying eyes," he said. "It is time to put this valuable tool to work for peace and for the security of our forces."

Any decision to deploy the EC-130E would have to originate from the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and its so-called Stabilisation Force, which includes British, German and American troops patrolling Bosnia, Pentagon officials said. They declined to discuss possible future operations.

Commando Solo was used during the 1991 Gulf War to broadcast so-called "Voice of the Gulf" programmes aimed at persuading Iraqi invaders of Kuwait to surrender. The aircraft was also used to override local broadcasts during U.S. interventions in Grenada (1983), Panama (1989) and Haiti (1994).

The Lockheed Martin Corp.-built Commando Solo aircraft belongs to the U.S. Air National Guard, which has six of them in inventory. Air-refuelable, it may broadcast in the standard AM, FM, HF, TV and military communications bands, an Air Force fact sheet said.
